content.text: A model doesn't get unrelated features for free: it has to learn to ignore them from a limited number of rows, and some models can't ignore them at all. On scikit-learn's breast cancer data, 100 unrelated columns drop k-nearest neighbors from 0.965 to 0.917 accuracy. Add features deliberately, and select them inside cross-validation.

A diagnostics team has a k-nearest neighbors model built on 30 tumor measurements, with a cross-validated accuracy of 0.965. A data engineer joins 100 more columns from the data warehouse: "The model will figure out what's useful." None of the new columns has anything to do with the diagnosis, and accuracy falls to 0.917. Nothing crashed, no warning appeared, and the new pipeline is bigger and slower to boot.
Many developers assume that adding features gives the model more information and can only help. The reasoning is appealing:

items.text: A model can always ignore a useless feature by giving it a weight of zero, so extra columns look free.
"More data is better" feels like it should apply to columns as well as rows.
Some models really are fairly tolerant: tree ensembles and regularized linear models often shrug off a few weak features, which reinforces the instinct.

content.text: ignore a useless feature. In practice it has to learn that the feature is useless, from the same limited rows, and it learns that imperfectly. Some models don't learn per-feature weights at all.
Every feature is something the model must either use or learn to ignore, and both cost something.
A model has to learn what to ignore

A model estimates its weights from the training rows, and in a finite sample even a random column lines up with the target by chance here and there. So a useless feature gets a small, nonzero role fitted to those coincidences: that's

, one column at a time. scikit-learn's permutation importance example shows it clearly: it adds a column of random numbers to the Titanic data, and a random forest's built-in importance ranks it among the most important features, because the forest has enough capacity to use it to overfit.

Google's Rules of Machine Learning give the budget in one line: the number of feature weights you can learn in a linear model is roughly proportional to the amount of data you have. Its example for a small dataset: 1,000 examples, a dozen features.
k-nearest neighbors has no weights to turn down. It predicts from the training rows closest to the new one, and the distance adds up differences across all columns. After

, every column counts the same, so with 30 real columns and 100 unrelated ones, most of each distance comes from columns that say nothing about the tumor. The "nearest" neighbors are increasingly chosen by noise.

tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)  # 30 real measurements
extra = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(len(X), 100))  # unrelated
X_all = np.hstack([X, extra])  # "the model will figure out what's useful"
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier())
for name, data in [("30 features", X), ("130 features", X_all)]:
    score = cross_val_score(knn, data, y, cv=cv).mean()
    print(f"{name:<12} accuracy {score:.3f}")
# 30 features  accuracy 0.965
# 130 features accuracy 0.917

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
extra = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(len(X), 100))
X_all = np.hstack([X, extra])
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(f_classif),
                     KNeighborsClassifier())
search = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"selectkbest__k": [10, 20, 40, 80, 130]}, cv=5)
score = cross_val_score(search, X_all, y, cv=cv).mean()  # k picked per fold
print(f"130 features, selection inside CV: accuracy {score:.3f}")
kept = search.fit(X_all, y).best_estimator_[1].get_support()
print(f"kept {kept.sum()} columns, {kept[30:].sum()} of them noise")
# 130 features, selection inside CV: accuracy 0.963
# kept 20 columns, 0 of them noise

content.text: Same model, same rows, and 100 extra columns cost almost five points of accuracy. The model has more information in the sense that the old columns are still there. It just can't find them under the new ones.
The scikit-learn nearest neighbors guide says it directly: in high-dimensional spaces, the method becomes less effective due to the so-called

. As dimensions grow, the space grows so fast that the same number of rows covers it ever more thinly, and "near" stops meaning much. Speed suffers too: the guide notes that KD-tree search, very fast below about 20 dimensions, becomes inefficient as dimensions grow.

Distance-based models feel it first, but not alone. In scikit-learn's univariate feature selection example, 20 noise columns are added to the 4 iris measurements. A linear SVM on all 24 scores 0.789; after keeping the 4 best features, 0.868. Without selection, the example observes, the SVM puts large weights on the real features but also uses many of the non-informative ones.

How to apply it in your project

items.title: Start from a baseline you trust

content.text: Measure a model on the features you understand, then add new columns in groups and keep only the groups that improve the cross-validated score.

items.title: Watch the ratio of features to rows

content.text: Google's rule of thumb for a thousand rows is about a dozen features. Hundreds of columns on that much data asks the model to find signal in noise.

items.title: Match the model to the width

The Rules of ML call unused features technical debt. Remove them from the pipeline and the data feeds, not just from the model.

items.text: Extra features aren't free: the model must learn to ignore each one, and finite data makes that imperfect.
Distance-based models suffer most: 100 unrelated columns took KNN from 0.965 to 0.917 accuracy.
The data you need grows with the number of features, the core of the curse of dimensionality.
